title: No general definition of intelligence independent of human details

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No general definition of intelligence independent of human details

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: General features proposed as marks of intelligence (learning and memory, adaptation, abstraction) occur in systems such as simple cellular automata and fluids, so there is no workable general definition of intelligence; any usable one must be tied to specific details of human intelligence.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: My guess is that ultimately there is not, and that in fact any workable definition of what we normally think of as intelligence will end up having to be tied to all sorts of seemingly rather specific details of human intelligence.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Intelligence in the Universe” (from p. 822), p. 823. Scope: definitions of intelligence

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-46: not-empirically-resolvable, resolvability 0.26

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Examples of learning, memory, or abstraction in simple systems can refute particular definitions but cannot establish the nonexistence of every general definition. The final requirement of human-specific detail is conceptual rather than a discriminating empirical prediction.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Catalog proposed intelligence definitions and test whether selected nonhuman systems satisfy their criteria, but no finite survey can prove that no workable general definition exists or decide which definition captures ordinary usage.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The claim quantifies over all possible definitions.

Shared features do not logically preclude a different general definition.

Workability and normal intelligence are normative criteria.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.35
operationalizability: 0.18
data existence: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.15
data adequacy: 0.2

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Memory-like persistence in a cellular automaton or a fluid is easy to simulate and puts pressure on particular proposed marks of intelligence. The sentence concludes that every workable definition must collapse into human particulars. Failed proposals do not distinguish that conclusion from the existence of a definition not yet stated.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For each candidate feature, such as learning, adaptation, or abstraction, either exhibit it in a system nobody counts as intelligent or show that humans lack it. Any finite list of features leaves open whether some other general definition works.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A proposed definition can be revised after each counterexample.

Workable, and what we normally think of as intelligence, are judgments.
